Cincinnati's best path runs through a New Orleans defense that struggles on third down and in the red zone. Quick throws against the blitz, third-and-medium conversions, and red-zone efficiency will likely decide the game.

sections.heading: Opponent defense
sections.body: New Orleans blitzes on 37.5% of dropbacks [dc5], fifth-highest in the league [dc6], so expect five-plus rushers and plan quick game and hot throws. Its pressure proxy is 14.7% [dc3], while Cincinnati's offense allows sacks on 4.7% of dropbacks [dc8]. Third down is the defense's weakest area: it allows conversions on 46.5% of third downs [dc15], ranked 29th [dc17], and Cincinnati converts 50.0% [dc18], so third-and-medium is the situation to attack. The run defense allows double-digit gains on 9.8% of runs [dc12] with 6.6 defenders in the box on average [dc14], so the run fits are where Cincinnati can find chunk gains. Overall New Orleans allows 0.04 EPA per play [dc23], ranked 20th [dc24].

sections.heading: Special teams
sections.body: New Orleans is average at range, making 70.0% of field goals [kc1] on 20 attempts [kc2] and 54.5% from 50-plus [kc3] on 11 attempts [kc4]. Carlson made 8 [kc5] of 12 [kc6] before Smyth took over, and Smyth has made 6 [kc7] of 8 [kc8] since, a thin sample, so do not assume Smyth matches Carlson's range. Late in a close game, the long-range mark argues for forcing a long attempt rather than conceding points. The punter averages 38.8 [kc9] yards per punt, but only 36.8% [kc11] land inside the 20, and kickoffs are touchbacks just 14.3% [kc12] of the time, so plan on returns. New Orleans punt coverage allows 8.1 [kc14] yards per return, against 4.3 [kc16] for Cincinnati's returners, so a fair catch is the default unless a return is needed. Cincinnati's kicker has made 93.8% [kc22] of 16 [kc23] attempts, so a long attempt is a credible late-game option.

sections.heading: Injuries and availability
sections.body: New Orleans lists safety Justin Reid Out [ic1], cornerback Martin Emerson Out [ic2] and center Erik McCoy Out [ic3]. Reid has played 89.9% of snaps [ic4] over 9 games [ic5], so backups will absorb safety snaps, and Emerson's 46.3% snap share [ic6] over 8 games [ic7] points to a rotation role in the secondary. McCoy's absence hits the interior pass protection. For Cincinnati, guard Dalton Risner is Out [ic8] after playing 93.6% of snaps [ic9] over 9 games [ic10], and receiver Andrei Iosivas is Doubtful [ic11]. Iosivas's 57.0% snap share [ic12] comes from only 2 games [ic13], a small sample. Ja'Marr Chase holds a 25.9% target share [ic14] on 371 team targets [ic15], so the passing plan runs through Chase regardless of Iosivas.

sections.heading: Key matchups
sections.body: Four matchups will decide this game. First, the quick game against the blitz: New Orleans sends five-plus rushers on 37.5% of dropbacks [mc1], fifth-highest in the league [mc2], while Cincinnati's sack rate is 4.7% of dropbacks [mc4], so lean on quick game and hot throws. Second, third down: Cincinnati converts 50.0% [mc5], while New Orleans allows 46.5% [mc6] over 129 third-down plays [mc7], ranked 29th [mc8]. Third, the run fits: New Orleans allows double-digit gains on 9.8% of runs [mc9] and puts 6.6 defenders in the box [mc10], so use the run to stay ahead of schedule. Fourth, coverage on Olave, who takes 27.8% of targets [mc11] while New Orleans is passing 1.3 percentage points above expectation [mc12]; Cincinnati allows explosive pass plays on 9.5% of attempts [mc13], so the secondary must limit the back end.
